title: The SoftBank Caper
subtitle: Six months before his arrest, Epstein was the shared intelligence node between the two Big Law firms circling opposite sides of the Misra-Benedetti dirty-tricks scandal
style_angle: The interesting thing about 'the Softbank caper' is not the honey trap — it is the lawyer-broker geometry around it

findings.summary: Ron Soffer (born Nov 12, 1960, Tel Aviv) is a Paris-based international litigation attorney. Founder of Soffer Avocats (est. 1994). Admitted to bars in Israel (1984), New York (1990), and Paris (1992). Hebrew University School of Law (1982). Speaks English, French, Hebrew. Served 5 years as officer in International Law Branch of the IDF Judge Advocate General. Admitted to act before the International Criminal Court (The Hague). Has presented cases to the European Court of Human Rights and teaches ECHR jurisprudence at Hebrew University. Practice areas include criminal cases, art law, international human rights, European law, securities litigation, banking law.

Ron Soffer identified: born Nov 12, 1960 in Tel Aviv, Israel. Founded Cabinet Ron Soffer (now Soffer Avocats) in Paris 1994. Admitted to bars in Israel (1984), New York (1990), Paris (1992). Served 5 years as officer in International Law Branch of IDF Judge Advocate General. Teaches ECHR jurisprudence at Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Practice includes multi-jurisdictional criminal/civil litigation across France, US, Germany, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Hungary, Morocco, Hong Kong, Singapore. Firm handles ECHR litigation, art law (Nazi restitution via Agnes Peresztegi), criminal defense, antitrust, securities.

Ron Soffer (born Nov 12, 1960, Tel Aviv) is the founder of Soffer Avocats, a Paris-based international litigation boutique established in 1994. Member of Paris (1992), New York (1990), Israel (1984), and Split (Croatia) bars. Admitted to practice before the ICC at The Hague. Hebrew University law degree (1982). Served 5 years as officer in the International Law Branch of the IDF Judge Advocate General. Teaches annually at Hebrew University on ECHR jurisprudence. Member of scientific committee of criminal law institute of Paris Bar. Writes for Israel Hayom and JNS.org.

FULL BIOGRAPHY SYNTHESIS: Benedetti (born Jul 1961, Italian, resident Switzerland/Geneva/Lugano) is a Geneva-based financier and founding partner of Schwarzfield. His career-defining deal: brokering the 2005 acquisition of Wind Telecomunicazioni SpA for Naguib Sawiris (Egyptian billionaire, Orascom Telecom), Europe's then-largest LBO at approx 12 billion euros. Benedetti received 67M+ euros but sued Sawiris for a 1/3 stake -- lost at UK Supreme Court Jul 2013 (Benedetti v Sawiris). Also investigated by Roman prosecutors for corruption in the Wind deal (2008). He has 30+ years experience in telecoms, energy, mining, real estate across W/E Europe, Scandinavia, CIS, Africa, North America, Middle East. Former non-exec director of Cadogan Petroleum (Ukraine oil/gas, Aug 2010-Jun 2012). Chairman of SPQR Capital SA. CEO of SAE Capital. Executive Chairman of NYSE-listed Equus Total Return (2011-2014).

DISAMBIGUATION: Alessandro De Benedetti at Northzone VC (grandson of Carlo De Benedetti/Olivetti/CIR dynasty, son of Marco De Benedetti/Carlyle) is a DIFFERENT person from Epstein's contact. Northzone De Benedetti is too young (joined as associate in 2024) and based in Stockholm. Epstein's Benedetti is the SAE Capital CEO born July 1961, confirmed via UK Companies House directorships and ICIJ Paradise Papers (Florence address).

ATTALI INVESTMENT PARTNERS LTD (UK 07138407): Benedetti was co-director with Bertrand Gauquelin des Pallieres (French, born Nov 1966, resident in Rome at 9 Via G A Rayneri). Company name references Jacques Attali -- former adviser to French President Mitterrand, founder of EBRD, head of Attali and Associates advisory firm. Benedetti and Gauquelin co-founded in Jan 2010, both resigned Dec 2015 (same month), replaced by METHORIOS CAPITAL LLP as corporate director. SIC code 64999 (financial intermediation). Registered at 43-45 Dorset Street London W1U. The Attali connection places Benedetti in elite Franco-Italian political and financial circles -- the same milieu as Epstein's Paris network.

IDF JAG background: Soffer served 5 years as officer in the International Law Branch of the Judge Advocate General of the IDF. He 'worked on dozens of cases presented to the Israeli Supreme Court on issues of laws of war' (per firm website). No specific cases, units, or commanding officers identified in public sources. No public reporting links Soffer to intelligence work (Mossad, Shin Bet, AMAN) -- search for 'Ron Soffer intelligence OR Mossad' returned zero results. The IDF JAG International Law Branch handles laws of armed conflict, Geneva Conventions compliance, and represents IDF in Supreme Court petitions -- a legal rather than intelligence function, though personnel may have security clearances and work with classified material.
findings.detail: IDF Military Advocate General's Corps (MAG Corps) International Law Branch is responsible for advising IDF on international humanitarian law, laws of armed conflict, rules of engagement, and representing the military in Supreme Court proceedings. Soffer served there approximately 1982-1987 based on his Israel Bar admission (1984) and move to New York (1988). This was during the 1982 Lebanon War and its aftermath -- a period of intense international law challenges for the IDF including the Sabra and Shatila massacre inquiry and numerous Supreme Court petitions. No public source identifies specific cases Soffer worked on. Web search for intelligence connections (Mossad, national security) returned zero results linking Soffer to any intelligence agency. However, IDF JAG officers routinely work with classified information and maintain security clearances.

Benedetti's claimed Jewish identity from ~1986 is self-presented, NOT ancestral — born/raised Catholic to Franzoni family ('cattolicissima'); reframes Weingarten's 'Italian jewish neighbor' description
findings.detail: Per Il Sole 24 Ore reconstruction by investigative journalist Claudio Gatti (Mar 11, 2008), Alessandro Benedetti was born and raised Catholic. Mother from the Franzoni family, described as 'cattolicissima' (extremely devout Catholic). However, from circa 1986 he allegedly began claiming Jewish identity, reportedly stating that 'great business deals require being Jewish.' This is what Reid Weingarten was relaying when he described Benedetti to Epstein on Dec 9, 2011 (EFTA00925685) as Epstein's 'Italian jewish neighbor on ave. foch.' NEGATIVE on documentary evidence that Benedetti is halakhically or ancestrally Jewish. NEGATIVE on connection to historic Italian Jewish patriciate families (Sereni, De Benedetti, Della Pergola, Foa, Modigliani). His Florence address (Via delle Serre 9/A) is non-historic-ghetto residential. Likely a claimed identity used as elite-network lubricant, particularly relevant given Benedetti's Sawiris (Egyptian Coptic), Saudi PIF/MBS-adjacent (via Misra/SoftBank), and Russian-language operational portfolio. Important disambiguation: Alessandro Benedetti is NOT related to the De Benedetti industrial dynasty (Carlo De Benedetti / Olivetti / CIR / GEDI) — his family was a failed crane-manufacturing concern from Sassuolo.

findings.summary: FL SunBiz records show Sunflower Properties Inc (P16061), a Delaware foreign profit corp registered in FL Sept 23, 1987, with principal address 'C/O Jeffrey B. findings.detail: This is the only corporate registration found in our registry.db that directly references the Paul Weiss law firm address. Sunflower Properties as a Delaware corp registered in Florida through PW's real estate partner Samuels in 1987-88 is consistent with the firm's extensive real estate practice. No other Paul Weiss LLP registrations were found in FL, NY, NM, CO, DC, or CA corporate registries — law firm LLPs are typically registered only in their state of formation (NY). Address search for 1285 Avenue of the Americas timed out (large dataset).

findings.summary: Republic National Bank of New York (1988-1991): Soffer worked in banking law at Edmond Safra's Republic National Bank before founding his Paris practice. Republic National Bank was founded by Edmond J. Safra (Lebanese-Brazilian-Israeli banker), later sold to HSBC for $10.3B in 1999. Safra died in a suspicious fire in Monaco Dec 1999. The bank was a major institution in the Israeli/Sephardic banking world with deep Middle East and Latin American connections. Soffer's 3-year tenure there (1988-1991) preceded his Paris career and overlaps with his New York Bar admission (1990).
findings.detail: Ron Soffer moved to New York in 1988 to join Republic National Bank of New York where he worked until 1991. Republic National Bank was Edmond Safra's flagship US institution. Safra was one of the wealthiest bankers in the world with extensive Middle East, Latin American, and European connections. The bank operated 80 branches in the NY metro area. Safra's death in Monaco (Dec 3, 1999 fire) remains controversial. The FBI has records on Safra and Republic National Bank. Soffer's banking law background at this institution is consistent with his later practice areas (banking law, corporate finance, international contracts) and his tri-jurisdictional career (Israel-US-France). This also provides context for the Fisher & Soffer partnership at 34 E 69th St -- Soffer was practicing law in NY during the same period Epstein leased the building (1992).

findings.summary: FARA records document 5 Paul Weiss registrations spanning 1963-2002, representing 14 foreign principals across 8 countries. Foreign clients: Government of Israel (1965-1966), Government of Morocco (1963), Government of Poland (1990), Government of Botswana (1987-1989), NEC/Nippon Electric (Japan, 1982-1996 across 3 registrations), Hyundai Heavy Industries (S. Korea, 1987-1989), Samsung Ship Building (S. Korea, 1986-1988), Korea Federation of Textile Industries (1985-1986), Korea Iron & Steel Assn (1985-1986), Embassy of Republic of Korea (1995-2000), Korea Telecom (1995-2001), Consolidated Gold Fields PLC (UK, 1988-1989), Le Groupe du Soleil (Canada, 1991-1992), Canadian Pulp & Paper Assn (1991-1992), Grupo Empresarial Agricola Mexicano (1992-1993).
findings.detail: The FARA history reveals three phases: (1) Cold War era (1963-66): Government representation for Israel and Morocco — both sensitive geopolitical clients. (2) Trade defense era (1982-1990): Heavy Korean industrial representation (4 principals), Japanese electronics (NEC), British mining (Consolidated Gold Fields during Minorco hostile takeover), Polish government (post-Communist transition). (3) Telecom/trade era (1991-2002): Korean telecom/government, Canadian lumber/trade disputes, Mexican agriculture (NAFTA era). The Government of Israel representation in 1965 is the earliest FARA registration and places the firm in Israel advocacy during the pre-Six Day War period. All registrations are terminated by 2002, suggesting the firm moved to unregistered foreign work or stopped foreign principal work entirely. Notable: the Korean representation is the deepest — 6 separate Korean principals across 16 years.

Ron Soffer full profile from Soffer Avocats: Born Israel 1960. Hebrew University School of Law 1981. Israel Bar 1984. In 1992, Epstein leased 34 East 69th Street (former Iranian Deputy Consul General residence seized by US State Dept Office of Foreign Missions) for $15,000/month. In 1996, Epstein sublet the building to criminal defense attorney Ivan S. Fisher for $20,000/month (pocketing $5K/month). Fisher sublet portions to several subtenants including Ron Soffer, operating as 'Fisher & Soffer a/k/a Fisher & Sophir.' The US sued for ejectment in Nov 1996 (SDNY 1:96-cv-08307, Judge Denny Chin). Epstein separately sued Fisher (SDNY 1:97-cv-01489). This places Soffer in Epstein's physical orbit in the mid-1990s, sharing office space in an Epstein-controlled building on the Upper East Side.

Soffer was a NAMED DEFENDANT (not counsel) in US v. Epstein, 96 Civ 8307 (DC). Represented himself pro se. Ejected by summary judgment Apr 1, 1998. (2) 2008-ongoing: SIPC v. Epstein v. Fisher holdover proceedings (SDNY 1:97-cv-01489, Judge Denny Chin): Filed Mar 5, 1997, terminated Mar 31, 2000. Cause: 28:1443(1) Removal from State Court - Civil Rights: Rent, Lease, and Ejectment. Epstein initiated holdover proceedings in NYC Civil Court against Fisher for nonpayment of rent under the sublease (Fisher had stopped paying rent after Sept 1996 AUSA meeting). Fisher removed to federal court; Judge Chin granted consolidation with the government's ejectment action (96-cv-8307). This case is significant because it confirms: (1) Epstein treated the Iranian consular property as income property (profiting $5K/month markup), (2) Fisher stopped paying when informed the sublease was illegal, (3) Epstein pursued legal claims against Fisher even after the government moved to eject them all. The Soffer reference in this docket is the same Apr 9, 1998 show-cause order cross-filed from 96-cv-8307.

Ron Soffer was a defendant in 96 CIV 8307 as a subtenant at 34 East 69th Street. He was listed as a resident of New York and France, and was part of Fisher & Soffer a/k/a Fisher & Sophir (Ivan Fisher's law partnership). Soffer was one of two holdout subtenants (with Diane Fisher) against whom the government sought partial summary judgment in March 1998 (EFTA01325003). This places Soffer in Epstein's physical orbit as early as 1996. Soffer later appears in the Jan 2019 Weingarten-Epstein email exchanges regarding the SoftBank matter.

Full docket reconstruction of US v. Epstein (SDNY 1:96-cv-08307): Second Amended Complaint (Dec 1997) named 17 defendants including Epstein, Fisher, Fisher & Soffer, and Ron Soffer individually. Judge Chin's Apr 1, 1998 opinion (1998 WL 159055) granted summary judgment for ejectment of all defendants. Soffer was the last holdout subtenant, declining the stipulation signed by all others. Key details: Epstein leased 34 E 69th St from OFM on Feb 1, 1992 at $15K/month, abandoned Jan 3, 1996, sublet to Fisher May 7, 1996 at $20K/month despite OFM denial. Fisher further sublet to multiple attorneys and businesses including Fisher & Soffer. The property was the former Iranian Deputy Consul General residence, making occupants trespassers on Iranian government property under US custodianship. Soffer registered the address with NY State Office of Court Administration for attorney registration purposes. Case terminated Mar 17, 1999.

LDA lobbying records reveal Paul Weiss operated as both a registered lobbying firm (1999-2000) and hired external lobbyists. As registrant: lobbied for IBP ($180K), SkyBridge LP ($100K), Natl Music Publishers Assn ($60K), CGFNS ($40K), Intelsat ($40K), Devereux Foundation ($40K), SpaceData ($10K), Owens-Corning, Coalition of Utility Cos, General Atlantic Service Corp. As client: hired Ernst & Young/Washington Council (2001-2002, $220K total) for own lobbying needs, hired ACG Advocacy (2019-2021, $600K+) on behalf of Qualcomm, and hired SKDKNICKERBOCKER (2019, $490K) on behalf of Carlos Ghosn.
findings.detail: Three distinct lobbying patterns: (1) Paul Weiss as direct registrant in 1999-2000 — predominantly meat industry (IBP, later acquired by Tyson), telecom (Intelsat), media (NMPA), and utilities. (2) Paul Weiss hiring lobbyists for itself — Ernst & Young Washington Council in 2001-2002 for unspecified advocacy. (3) Paul Weiss hiring lobbyists on behalf of clients — ACG Advocacy for Qualcomm antitrust issues (K/quarter, 2019-2021) and SKDKNICKERBOCKER for Ghosn media campaign (K in 2019 alone). The Qualcomm lobbying coincides with Broadcom hostile takeover defense (2019). The SkyBridge LP client is notable — SkyBridge Capital is Anthony Scaramucci's firm.

Benedetti's pre-SoftBank legal exposure: June 2003 Turin conviction (1 year 7 months reclusione, suspended) for Commertec bankruptcy; UK Supreme Court loss to Sawiris (2013); Sept 1996 Nice police raid
findings.detail: Alessandro Benedetti (Italian, born July 13, 1961, Sassuolo Modena; resident Lugano 7 Riva Paradiso) had substantial pre-SoftBank legal exposure: (1) June 12, 2003: Turin conviction for Commertec bankruptcy — 1 year 7 months reclusione (suspended). First documented Italian criminal conviction. (2) July 17, 2013: UK Supreme Court loss to Naguib Sawiris (Wind Telecom brokerage fee dispute, ~€67M plus €3.4M support = ~€97M total). Benedetti v Sawiris [2013] UKSC 50 became the leading UK precedent on unjust enrichment / quantum meruit. Lower courts: UK High Court 2009, Court of Appeal 2010. (3) September 1996: Nice judicial police raided his Beaulieu-sur-Mer residence (Villa Roc Fleuri); subsequent French imprisonment and house arrest (per Il Sole 24 Ore reconstruction by Claudio Gatti, Mar 11 2008). (4) February 28, 2008: Rome prosecutors opened bribery investigation into the Wind deal naming Naguib Sawiris, Fulvio Conti (Enel CEO), and Benedetti as mediator. Outcome likely time-barred (prescrizione). (5) 2014 UK Commercial Court: Kruppa v Benedetti [2014] EWHC 1887 (Comm) — joint defendant with Bertrand des Pallieres. By 2015 when Misra hired him, Benedetti had 30+ years of cross-jurisdictional financial-intelligence tradecraft and a documented Italian criminal record.

findings.summary: Comprehensive US financial/corporate footprint search yielded ZERO results across 14 databases: no US corporate entities (FL, NY, NM, PA registries), no SEC EDGAR filings, no NYC property records, no UCC filings, no FAA aircraft, no lobbying registrations, no FARA foreign agent registrations, no OCCRP Aleph records, no LittleSis entries, no nonprofit organizations. Only US financial trace: single $1,000 FEC donation in 2007. This near-total absence from US registries is consistent with a lawyer whose practice is headquartered in Paris and operates primarily in European/international jurisdictions. It means any financial arrangements involving Soffer would be conducted through French or offshore entities, outside the reach of these US-focused databases.

findings.summary: 10-YEAR PREQUEL TO THE SOFTBANK CAPER — Benedetti himself brokered the underlying deal. The 'Egyptian investor' to whom Apax/TPG sold TIM Hellas for EUR 3.4bn in Feb 2007 is Naguib Sawiris/Weather Investments (later renamed Wind Telecom S.p.A.). Per existing finding #861, Benedetti's career-defining deal was brokering Sawiris's 2005 acquisition of Wind Telecomunicazioni SpA — Europe's largest LBO at ~EUR 12bn — for which Benedetti received EUR 67M+ but sued Sawiris for a 1/3 stake and lost at UK Supreme Court [2013] UKSC 50 (Benedetti v Sawiris). The TIM Hellas litigation (Hosking/Bonney NY claim and Luxembourg suit) used in Oct 2015 to smear Arora arose directly from a deal that BENEDETTI BROKERED to Sawiris in 2007. The 2015 Independent piece is therefore not just a planted smear — it is Benedetti weaponizing the unwind of his own brokered deal to attack the man he was paid USD 500K to destroy. The structural grievance loop: (1) 2005 Benedetti brokers Wind for Sawiris, gets EUR 67M; (2) 2007 Sawiris/Wind acquires TIM Hellas from Apax/TPG; (3) 2009 TIM Hellas collapses; (4) 2013 UKSC rules against Benedetti; (5) 2015 Misra pays Benedetti USD 500K to use the TIM Hellas litigation as ammunition against Arora. Benedetti has personal grievance against Sawiris AND structural knowledge of every transaction in the chain. He is the only operative who could have curated this exact attack vector.

ProPublica 990 records reveal the Mark & Stephanie Madoff Foundation (EIN 26-1445331) listed its address as 'C/O Paul Weiss, 1285 Avenue of the Americas, New York NY 10019-6064'. Filed 990-PFs from 2007-2017 as a 501(c)(3). The foundation had $1.8M in assets in 2011-2012, received $566K revenue in 2014, then spent $2.1M in 2014 expenses (apparent wind-down), dropping to $113K assets by 2015. Mark Madoff (Bernie Madoff's son) died by suicide in December 2010. Paul Weiss served as custodial address for the foundation through its dissolution.
findings.detail: The Madoff Foundation C/O Paul Weiss connection is noteworthy for several reasons: (1) Paul Weiss was involved in Madoff-related litigation, representing some victims. (2) The foundation continuing operations under PW's custodial address through 2017, seven years after Mark Madoff's death, suggests PW served as dissolution counsel. (3) The $2.1M expense spike in 2014 likely represents final distributions or legal costs. (4) Also found in 990 search: The Aftermath Project Inc (EIN 20-2740495, Los Angeles) — appears to be a separate arts nonprofit, not PW-connected.

Cause: strategic over-aggressiveness on valuations. SIGNIFICANCE: India complaint significant NOT as regulatory matter (closed) but as operational signature of Misra dirty-tricks apparatus. Giannakopoulos = SCL Switzerland linkage ties Misra's operation directly into Cambridge Analytica / SCL Group network — same infrastructure that operated against 1MDB Malaysia, reportedly worked Indian elections for BJP, and Trump 2016 US. NEW ENTITIES TO RESEARCH: Kensington Capital International (BVI), Beacon Vatika Holdings Limited (Mauritius), CH Communication SA (Geneva, Charles Ergen/Dish JV repurposed), Mintz & Gold LLP NY (engaged alongside Boies Schiller), Raine Group/Raine Partners (Sama conflict).

Listed in ICIJ Offshore Leaks database.

The structure confirms Epstein's exact description in EFTA02625442: 'R has a bvi co. xitrans. that is owned by a family trust. (cyprus).' Xitrans (BVI) -> The Virgo Trust (Cyprus) -> Rybolovlev (beneficiary). The Virgo Trust transferred through Merco Trustees at Neocleous House, a standard Cyprus trust administration arrangement.

Epstein demonstrated precise knowledge of Rybolovlev's offshore structure in Jan 15 2019 email (EFTA02625442 to Ruemmler, forwarded to Wolff as EFTA02625537). The level of detail (BVI incorporation, Cyprus trust, family trust structure) goes well beyond public reporting available at the time. Sotheby's (SDNY 1:18-cv-09011). The email was sent to Kathy Ruemmler (former White House Counsel, then Goldman Sachs General Counsel) and Michael Wolff (journalist) — suggesting Epstein was positioning this intelligence for use in either legal proceedings or media exposure.

Cypress Hill LLC (DC0128296) represents a clear successor pattern to the dissolved Cypress Inc (581974). Three months later, Cypress Hill LLC registered 03/26/2024 with BBVI as agent at same Royal Palms address but with all@bizusvi.com email (not Brett's personal). Purpose: Other, Other. Principal office: Royal Palms (not 6100 Red Hook). The 3-month gap between dissolution and new registration, identical agent, and Cypress naming convention strongly indicate intentional succession. However, the shift from 6100 Red Hook (Epstein property) to Royal Palms (BBVI office) as principal office, and from Inc to LLC form, suggest either: (1) a restructured entity for estate wind-down, (2) a new purpose entity using salvaged naming, or (3) a non-Epstein BBVI client using generic plant nomenclature.

BBVI infrastructure continues active operations as of February 2026 with three distinct operational threads: (1) ONGOING MAINTENANCE: BBVI itself (582110) In Good Standing with AR 2025 filed Apr 7 2025. Kellerhals Ferguson Kroblin PLLC (583297) In Good Standing with AR 2025. (DP0137481) registered Jan 28 2026 -- just 2 weeks ago -- as Erika Kellerhals sole professional corporation at 9053 Estate Thomas. The pattern shows: wind-down of legacy Epstein entities (Foundation dissolved), persistent maintenance of financial entities (Southern Financial repeatedly rescued from dissolution), and new entity formation through the same infrastructure. Kellerhals has rebranded her legal practice from partnership (Kellerhals Ferguson Kroblin) to solo P.C., suggesting either partner departure or strategic restructuring.

ILEX FIDUTRUST SA is a Geneva-based trust company at 6 Place des Eaux-Vives, Case Postale 3338, 1211 Geneve 3, Switzerland. It served as intermediary for Xitrans Finance Ltd (BVI #494095) and manages 241 total entities through Mossack Fonseca, primarily BVI and Panama companies. The firm functions as a classic Swiss trust administration company -- creating and managing offshore vehicles for wealthy clients through Panama's Mossack Fonseca law firm (exposed in Panama Papers 2016). ILEX managed Xitrans from its inception in 2002 through at least 2015 (Panama Papers data cutoff). The firm's role is administrative intermediary -- it does not own the entities but manages their corporate housekeeping, filings, and communications with the registered agent (Mossack Fonseca). This connects the Rybolovlev offshore structure to the broader network of Swiss-managed BVI/Panama entities that characterize post-Soviet oligarch wealth structures.

Corporation RICO case laundering mechanism used 8 FL shell companies: Trends Clothing Corp (FL L60041, Cabrerizo president, 1990-2007), Havana Club Wear Inc, Union Financial Research Inc (Rydz/Battle Jr, fake mortgage lender), YMR Corp, Biscayne Coast Investments, Ambar Industries, One Stop Properties Inc (FL S01616, still active), Key Financial Research Inc. The Corporation's textile-based money laundering (Trends Clothing, Havana Club Wear) and South Florida geographic overlap with Epstein operations are coincidental unless new evidence emerges. The 8 Corporation shell companies also return zero hits in the Epstein corpus. The Corporation's offshore laundering route (Panama/Curacao/BVI/European numbered accounts) uses some of the same jurisdictions as Epstein's offshore entities but through entirely separate mechanisms and entities.

findings.summary: Kuhn and Epstein discussed geopolitics as private business beyond the TV project. Kuhn wrote: 'We can always do Skype, of course' and 'Obviously, whenever we need to communicate privately about Radical Breakthroughs just email, Skype or meet. Also on other stuff, too.' Their calls included 'private, pick-me-up Skype/FaceTime on geopolitics' separate from project discussions. Kuhn explicitly distinguished 'private matters' from the Chaitin meeting. Topics discussed included Trump-Xi relations, China trade war, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, and the Silk Road. This suggests the TV project was not the sole basis of the relationship.

Formal corporate resolution for Nautilus Inc (EFTA01266733) documents the deliberate transition from Kellerhals Ferguson LLP to Business Basics VI LLC as registered agent. The resolution, signed by Jeffrey E. Epstein (President) and Darren Indyke (Secretary), states: 'the current agent for service of process of the Corporation, Kellerhals Ferguson LLP, hereby resigns as agent for service of process' and 'the Corporation hereby appoints, Business Basics VI LLC, as the new agent.' This was executed on September 13, 2012, with BBVI's initial address at 9100 Havensight, Port of Sale, Ste 15-16, St. Thomas VI 00802 (same as Kellerhals Ferguson LLP). The transition was notarized by Harry I. Beller, Notary Public State of New York (Commission No. 01814853924, Rockland County). This shows BBVI was purpose-built to replace the law firm as registered agent.

BBVI contact details from USVI Resident Agent Forms (multiple EFTAs): Phone: (340) 776-8812, Email: info@bizusvi.com, Physical: Royal Palms Professional Building, 62-3A & 62-3B Estate Thomas, Suite 101, St. Thomas VI 00802, Mailing: 9053 Estate Thomas Suite 101, St. Thomas VI 00802. Earlier address (pre-move, circa 2012): 9100 Havensight, Port of Sale, Suite 15-16, St. Thomas VI 00802 (shared with Kellerhals Ferguson LLP). A second phone (340) 779-2564 appears on earlier agent forms (Sept 2012). The address migration from Havensight to Royal Palms correlates with the firm's evolution from Kellerhals Ferguson LLP to standalone BBVI operations.

Brett Geary appears on USVI Division of Corporations personnel list (EFTA01363319) as 'GEARY, BRETT A A' at position #6, alongside TRAYNOR, CARA / ROBINSON, CARA (#5) and THOMAS, WILLIAM AVERY (#7). Separate document (EFTA01363318) lists FERGUSON, GREG J / FERGUSON, GREGORY J (#2), HANRATTY, THOMAS E (#3), and ROBINSON, KELLY M / TRAYNOR, KELLY (#4). These appear to be authorized corporate contacts associated with BBVI-serviced entities, listing all persons with signing authority or corporate roles. The presence of multiple individuals beyond the Kellerhals-Ferguson-Geary triad suggests BBVI maintained a small staff for managing entity filings.

Prytanee LLC Articles of Organization (EFTA01296058-60, Corp No. 586644) show Brett Geary as sole organizer, with BBVI as resident agent. Registered July 22, 2016, certified same date by Lt. Gov. Osbert E. Potter. Initial manager address is '6-04 Avenue Evenement' — a French address consistent with Prytanee being the art acquisition vehicle for Etienne Binant in Paris. The LLC was member-managed with initial capital of One Thousand Dollars (,000.00). Physical/mailing address: Royal Palms Professional Building, 62-3A & 62-3B Estate Thomas, Suite 101. This confirms Brett Geary personally organized entities with operational addresses in France, not just USVI.

Cross-database document inventory for BBVI: LMSBAND identifies 'Business Basics VI' as an ORG entity appearing in 60 files (67 total mentions). DugganUSA returns 1,000 hits for 'Business Basics' and 277 for 'Brett Geary.' LMSBAND returns 20+ documents for Brett Geary and 1 for Marcel Kellerhals. The Marcel Kellerhals reference (EFTA01269393) is a FirstBank banking form — the OCR renders 'Email' as 'Emit Marcel' — likely a false positive rather than a genuine Marcel Kellerhals reference. Marcel Kellerhals returns zero results in DOJ Vol 11, zero in Epstein 20K, and zero in Unified DB, despite 661 DugganUSA hits (per earlier finding #1367). This indicates Marcel appears primarily in DugganUSA-exclusive corporate filings, NOT in Epstein's personal correspondence or seized documents.

Zero financial transactions found for Business Basics VI LLC, Brett Geary, or Kellerhals in the DS10 Deutsche Bank dataset (579 transactions, $304M total). This is investigatively significant: it means BBVI fees and Kellerhals legal fees were NOT paid through the Deutsche Bank accounts captured in the SDNY grand jury subpoena. Payments likely flowed through separate banking channels (FirstBank VI is documented for Laurel Inc, EFTA01269393) or through inter-entity transfers within the STC ecosystem. Combined with zero results for bizusvi email addresses in DOJ Vol 11, this suggests BBVI's operational communications and financial dealings were deliberately segregated from Epstein's personal email accounts and DB banking.

Gratitude America Ltd received IRS 501(c)(3) tax-exempt determination (EFTA01365895) dated Sept 27, 2012, addressed to 9100 Havensight Port of Sale Ste 15, St Thomas VI 00802 -- the BBVI/Kellerhals Ferguson LLP address. Effective date April 25, 2012. Classified as private foundation under section 509(a). Contact: Sherry Q Wan (IRS). Separate Fedwire records (EFTA01273131-32) show Gratitude America received wires at this address: $150,000 (Dec 11, 2017) and $233,087.94 (date unclear, annotated 'TO CLOSE DB ACCOUNT'). Originator: Gratitude America Ltd C/O HBRK Associates Inc, 575 Lexington Avenue 4th Floor, New York NY 10022 (Indyke/Kahn entity). Wire routed from Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas to FirstBank Puerto Rico. This confirms BBVI's address served as the official IRS and banking address for Epstein's primary charitable vehicle.

Registry database confirms 14 entities with BBVI as registered agent -- ALL are known Epstein entities. Zero non-Epstein clients identified across all search sources (DOJ Vol 11, DugganUSA, LMSBAND, Unified DB, Epstein 20K, USVI registry, investigations DB). The 14 entities: Cypress Hill LLC (active), Cypress Inc (dissolved), Gratitude America Ltd (dissolved), IGO Company LLC (dissolved), J. Epstein VI Foundation Inc (dissolved), Jeepers Inc (admin dissolved), Laurel Inc (dissolved), LSJ Emergency LLC (dissolved), LSJE LLC (dissolved), Maple Inc (dissolved), Nautilus Inc (dissolved), Poplar Inc (dissolved), Southern Trust Company Inc (active), Zorro Management LLC (dissolved). This is consistent with BBVI being a single-client captive service entity, not a general-purpose registered agent. The 'business consultant' designation on STC's license may have been used to justify EDC tax benefits rather than reflecting actual multi-client consulting practice.

BBVI appears in ZERO federal litigation as a party despite managing 28+ Epstein USVI shell entities. Search for 'Business Basics' returned 20 results, all unrelated (Design Basics copyright cases, Kitchen Basics bankruptcy, etc.). Cases search returned 20 results with zero matches. Opinions search returned 10 results with zero matches. This is investigatively significant: a registered agent company managing a M+ corporate infrastructure with 28 entities has zero federal court footprint, suggesting effective legal insulation.

FARA search returned zero results for both 'Kellerhals' and 'Business Basics.' LDA search returned zero for 'Kellerhals' (one unrelated 'Dan Geary' result for 'Geary'). Given Kellerhals arranged meetings between Epstein and USVI political figures (Governor Mapp, gubernatorial candidate Bryan), had meetings 'on the Hill' in DC, and Epstein's network has documented FARA non-compliance across 15+ intermediaries, this absence is consistent with the broader pattern of shadow political influence without required disclosures.

BBVI confirmed absent from all offshore leak databases and sanctions lists. OCCRP Aleph: 20 results for 'Business Basics' but ZERO matches for BBVI (all unrelated companies). OpenSanctions: zero results for both 'Business Basics' and 'Kellerhals.' ICIJ database not searchable (Neo4j not installed), but Aleph (which includes ICIJ data) returned no matches. However, the absence from news databases is investigatively significant -- BBVI has maintained near-total media invisibility despite managing 28+ entities for the world's most notorious sex trafficker.

findings.summary: PATTERN ANALYSIS: Tony Sage corporate conduct exhibits recurring pattern across 20+ years — (1) share-for-asset swaps between controlled entities, (2) regulatory arbitrage when exchanges block deals, (3) payments through obscured channels, (4) offshore entity structures, (5) simultaneous control of multiple listed vehicles creating cross-holding networks
findings.detail:
COMPREHENSIVE PATTERN ANALYSIS of Tony Sage's corporate conduct across Cape Lambert, CuFe, European Lithium, CRML, Perth Glory, Cyclone Metals, Global Iron, International Petroleum:

PATTERN 1 — SHARE-FOR-ASSET SWAPS: Sage repeatedly acquires assets cheaply and vends them into listed vehicles for share consideration. Examples: (a) CopperCo acquired from receivership via debt-to-equity conversion, assets sold for ~A$300M; (b) Cape Lambert magnetite project bought for A$20M, sold to MCC for A$400M; (c) Kasombo project vended into Fe Limited for 25M shares + facilitator shares; (d) CRML copper powder: 40kg acquired for 2M shares at $10/share ($20M). The CRML deal is the outlier — it involves a physical commodity with disputed pricing (claimed $1,500-2,500/g vs market sources saying 2-3 orders of magnitude lower) rather than a mining tenement.

PATTERN 2 — REGULATORY ARBITRAGE: When ASX blocked Sage-Timis deals (Global Iron, International Petroleum) due to concerns about Timis' influence and continuous disclosure compliance, Sage listed both on the less-regulated NSX. When Sage needed a US listing for CRML's Greenland rare earth play, he used a BVI incorporation and SPAC merger rather than direct ASX listing.

PATTERN 3 — OBSCURED PAYMENT CHANNELS: Perth Glory salary cap: player payments routed through family member bank accounts. ATO investigation: $19.8M allegedly disguised as loans via offshore entities. In both cases, Sage claimed lack of knowledge of the specific arrangements.

PATTERN 4 — OFFSHORE STRUCTURES: Cape Lambert Corporation (Panama, Mossack Fonseca, 2007, intermediary Consulco International in RAK FTZ UAE) — name matches Sage's company but ICIJ database lists no officers. Metal Exploration Mauritius Ltd — Cape Lambert subsidiary. CRML — incorporated in BVI. Swiss Commodity Re — HK-based entity, Deayton has two BVI entities in ICIJ databases.

PATTERN 5 — CROSS-HOLDING NETWORK: Sage simultaneously chairs/controls CRML, European Lithium (holds 37.3% of CRML), CuFe, and (until Oct 2025) Cyclone Metals. All entities share the same registered address: 32 Harrogate Street, West Leederville WA. Okewood Pty Ltd provides consulting services to multiple entities. This creates a web where assets and value can flow between entities under Sage's control.

RELEVANCE TO CRML COPPER POWDER DEAL: The copper powder transaction ($20M in shares at 40% premium for 40kg of 99.96% pure copper powder from Swiss Commodity Re) resembles prior Sage transactions in form (share-for-asset swap) but differs in important ways: (a) the asset is a physical commodity, not a mining tenement; (b) the seller (Swiss Commodity Re / Kenneth Deayton) has no established connection to Sage, unlike prior related-party swaps; (c) the pricing is disputed by market sources; (d) there is no independent valuation disclosed; (e) 200K additional shares went to Malcolm Macintyre (Capella Capital), whose role as 'co-seller' is unexplained.

findings.detail:
COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS of CRML copper powder deal vs Sage's historical share-for-asset transactions:

SIMILARITIES: (1) Asset acquired for share consideration at a premium (CRML: 40% premium; Cape Lambert-FEL: shares at VWAP); (2) Non-cash transaction avoiding cash outflow from a cash-poor entity (CRML had $7.3M cash, $52M annual losses); (3) Shares issued in private placement exempt from registration; (4) Transaction creates paper value on balance sheet without cash expenditure.

CRITICAL DIFFERENCES: (1) VALUATION: Cape Lambert's mining tenement transactions had geological reports, resource estimates, and comparable transaction benchmarks. The copper powder has no disclosed independent valuation and market sources dispute the $1,500-2,500/g pricing as 2-3 orders of magnitude too high; (2) SELLER RELATIONSHIP: Prior deals (Kasombo, CopperCo, African Iron) involved identifiable mining industry counterparties. Swiss Commodity Re is a HK corporate services entity whose director Kenneth Deayton has no mining/commodities background — he's a CPA/Deloitte/HSBC veteran running corporate services; (3) REGULATORY OVERSIGHT: Cape Lambert's ASX deals were subject to ASX listing rules, continuous disclosure, and ASIC oversight. CRML is BVI-incorporated, NASDAQ-listed as a foreign private issuer — reducing regulatory scrutiny compared to ASX; (4) FACILITATOR SHARES: The Kasombo deal included 10M 'facilitator shares.' The copper powder deal includes 200K shares to Malcolm Macintyre — his role is equally opaque; (5) SCALE OF PREMIUM: A$20M for 40kg of copper powder (A$500K/kg) vs established market pricing suggests the transaction may be a mechanism to issue shares at a discount rather than a genuine commercial acquisition.

STRUCTURAL HYPOTHESIS: The copper powder deal may serve a similar function to Sage's prior share-for-asset swaps — creating paper asset value while issuing shares to specific parties — but the extreme pricing anomaly and lack of independent verification distinguish it from standard mining industry practice.

findings.summary: BVI incorporation pattern classic for Russian-origin VC-backed tech: tax-neutral holding with Russian dev, US sales, Irish/Singapore transfer pricing
findings.detail: The NGINX corporate structure follows a textbook BVI holding pattern for Russian-origin technology companies: (1) BVI parent entity for tax-neutral equity holding and investor-friendly jurisdiction, (2) US subsidiary (Delaware) for sales, marketing, and customer-facing operations at 795 Folsom St, SF, (3) Russian subsidiary (Moscow) retaining core engineering talent, (4) Ireland subsidiary (Cork) for European operations and potential IP/transfer pricing benefits, (5) Singapore subsidiary for Asia-Pacific sales. This structure allows: investor equity to be held in English common-law BVI jurisdiction (avoiding Russian corporate law complications), flexible repatriation of capital, tax-efficient intercompany arrangements via Ireland and Singapore, and straightforward acquisition structure (BVI merger under BVI Act rather than complex Russian M&A). The Series B-3 ($13.9M, 2017) and Series C ($43.3M, 2018) indicate the company raised approximately $105M total before the $670M exit.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Fraud claims fail Rule 9(b) - no specifics on who, what, when, where, how of alleged theft and evidence destruction
findings.detail: F5 Section I (pp.3-7) argues all fraud-based claims (Claims 1, 9, 10, 13-14, 18-24) fail Rule 9(b) heightened pleading. Key arguments: (1) Lynwood alleges in boilerplate fashion that NGINX Software Inc and NGINX BVI engaged in fraud by directing theft of Rambler equipment and destruction of evidence but fails to specify WHICH defendant stole WHAT equipment, WHERE, WHEN, and HOW; (2) Same deficiency for evidence destruction - fails to allege what actions were taken, who destroyed evidence, where, when, and how; (3) For F5 aiding-and-abetting fraud claim, Lynwood bases it on conclusory allegations F5 knew about and provided substantial assistance in achieving the sale of the NGINX Enterprise, but fails to specify what misrepresentations F5 knew about or how F5 assisted; (4) For trademark fraud claims (18-23), Lynwood fails to show that at the time trademark applications were signed, conflicting rights were clearly established or known to the signatory; (5) For false advertising (Claim 24), fails to identify specific misleading statements, which defendant made them, and when/where; (6) Critically, F5 argues Rambler was never entitled to rely on any alleged misrepresentations because Rambler was a sophisticated tech company that knew about NGINX popularity and paid Sysoev bonuses for it - if it relied on misrepresentations, it closed its eyes to the truth.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Lanham Act claims barred by laches - Rambler knew since 2004 but waited until 670M acquisition
findings.detail: F5 Section II.E (pp.13-15) argues laches bars all Lanham Act claims. Key facts: (1) Defendants openly used and registered NGINX marks for many years but Lynwood did nothing - that suddenly changed when F5 acquired NGINX BVI for 670M in 2019; (2) Conduct underlying claims began as early as 2004 when Sysoev allegedly released software under NGINX mark without authorization; (3) Even taking later dates: Dec 2011 departure, Aug 2012 first trademark registration, 2013 NGINX Plus commercial rollout - neither Lynwood nor Rambler took any action for 7+ years, far longer than any applicable limitations period; (4) Lynwood was aware of NGINX mark use via own allegations (paras 215, 282, 520); (5) Rambler had constructive notice of 2012 trademark registration; (6) In Jan 2015, Lynwood entered assignment agreement with Rambler after Sysoev appeared in media asserting NGINX authorship, yet still waited 5 more years. Prejudice: (1) NGINX BVI raised 100M in venture funding based primarily on NGINX Plus; (2) F5 allocated 14.5M to trade name and 509M to goodwill in 670M acquisition; (3) NGINX surpassed Apache in market share. F5 argues this rapid growth would have occurred under a different mark if Lynwood had not delayed.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: F5 could not have known about or aided 2011 wrongs when it acquired NGINX in 2019
findings.detail: F5 Section IV.C.2-3 (pp.27-29) makes a temporal impossibility argument against the aiding-and-abetting claim: (1) Lynwood theory is that by acquiring NGINX in May 2019, F5 substantially assisted Rambler former employees - all of whom ended employment with Rambler in 2011 or 2012 - to breach employment obligations and defraud Rambler; (2) But any fraud happened no later than 2011 and any employment duties ended in 2011-2012, so F5 Networks in 2019 could not have known about, much less assisted, wrongs that predated its involvement by nearly a decade; (3) Lynwood conclusory allegations that F5 knew about the wrongs are based only on boilerplate known or should have known assertions; (4) The few specifics Lynwood does allege actually REFUTE F5 knowledge: NGINX BVI warranted to F5 Networks that NGINX BVI owned the NGINX Software outright and that no NGINX BVI employee was breaching any duty owed to any former employer (Compl para 415); (5) Knowledge is the crucial element for aiding-and-abetting, and Lynwood fails to plead actual knowledge of the specific primary violation. Nowhere does Lynwood allege F5 actually knew of the former employees alleged misrepresentations or that the sale would breach NDA, work-for-hire, and disclosure obligations supposedly owed Rambler over seven years after employment ended.

findings.summary: F5's counter-narrative: Sysoev wrote first NGINX code in 2001 after ~1 year at Rambler as sysadmin; released open source in 2004 while still at Rambler; Rambler never objected, gave Sysoev salary increases and bonuses; NGINX surged to 6% global market share by 2010; Sysoev left Rambler in 2011 to work full-time on NGINX; Rambler never accused Sysoev of stealing or claimed ownership during 8-year period (2011-2019)
findings.detail: F5's Background section (Doc 88, pp.18-20) constructs a narrative emphasizing Rambler's knowledge and acquiescence. Key factual admissions by F5 (drawn from complaint allegations they do not contest): (1) Sysoev wrote first line of NGINX code in 2001 (Compl. para 11); (2) At that time he had worked at Rambler approximately one year as systems administrator; (3) In 2004, while still at Rambler, Sysoev published NGINX as open source code, free for anyone to download (Compl. para 21); (4) Rambler never objected or instructed Sysoev to remove NGINX from public domain; (5) Instead, Rambler gave Sysoev salary increases and paid him bonuses (Compl. paras 21, 191); (6) By 2010, NGINX had 6% global market share (Compl. para 173); (7) In 2011, Sysoev left Rambler to dedicate himself full-time to NGINX; (8) Former employees registered NGINXPLUS.COM domain in 2010 (Compl. paras 34, 232); (9) Former employees formed NGINX Software Inc. and NGINX Inc. (BVI) in 2011 (Compl. paras 273, 313-14, 337-38); (10) NGINX BVI raised $100M in venture funding based primarily on NGINX Plus product (Compl. para 47); (11) F5 Networks acquired NGINX companies for $670M in 2019 (Compl. paras 55, 404); (12) In the acquisition, $14.5M was allocated to trade name and $509M to goodwill (Compl. para 404-05). F5 emphasizes that Rambler never claimed ownership during the entire 8-year period from Sysoev's 2011 departure until F5's 2019 acquisition.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Key factual admissions - Sysoev employment dates, NGINX timeline, Rambler knowledge, and acquisition terms
findings.detail: F5 makes or accepts these factual statements in Doc 88: ADMITTED/ACCEPTED: (1) Sysoev was a Rambler employee from 2000 to 2011 (Glossary p.15); (2) Sysoev wrote first line of NGINX code in 2001 (p.19, citing Compl para 11); (3) NGINX was published as open source in 2004, while Sysoev was at Rambler (p.19); (4) Konovalov was Rambler employee 2008-2011 and co-founder of NGINX BVI (p.15); (5) Smirnoff was Rambler employee 2006-2012 and then NGINX BVI employee (p.15); (6) Dounin was Rambler employee 2004-2007 and later NGINX BVI employee (p.15); (7) NGINX BVI was incorporated in 2011 (p.15); (8) NGINX Software Inc registered first NGINX trademarks in 2011 (p.15); (9) NGINX BVI began developing NGINX Plus and licensed it from 2013 to 2019 (p.15); (10) F5 Networks acquired NGINX BVI and NGINX Software Inc in 2019 for 670M (p.19); (11) F5 concedes it is exploiting NGINX (p.36); (12) NGINX BVI raised 100M in venture funding based primarily on NGINX Plus (p.32, Compl para 47); (13) In acquisition, 14.5M allocated to trade name and 509M to goodwill (p.32); (14) Rambler assigned rights to Lynwood in Jan 2015 (p.31-32); (15) NGINX Plus was primary revenue driver for NGINX BVI from 2013 to 2019 (p.32, Compl para 47). DISPUTED: F5 does NOT accept that NGINX code was Rambler work-for-hire, that the Yam Server existed or was destroyed, or that any confidential information was misappropriated.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Yam Server and evidence destruction treated ONLY as Rule 9(b) pleading deficiency, not substantively addressed
findings.detail: F5's treatment of the Yam Server and evidence destruction allegations is notably superficial. The motion mentions these allegations only in Section I (fraud pleading, p.21) where it challenges them under Rule 9(b): Lynwood alleges NGINX Software Inc and NGINX BVI engaged in fraud by directing the theft of Rambler equipment and destruction of evidence (Compl para 682). F5 response is purely procedural - Lynwood fails to specify which defendant stole what equipment, where, when, and how; and fails to specify who destroyed evidence, where, when, and how. F5 does NOT substantively deny that equipment was stolen or evidence destroyed. It does NOT address the Yam Server by name. It does NOT explain what happened to the server. This is a conspicuous omission in a 53-page brief that argues every other point at length. The motion's silence on the merits of the Yam Server allegation is itself informative - F5 chose to attack only the pleading specificity rather than deny the factual allegations.

findings.summary: Doc 103-2 contains four separate RFPs dated 08/28/2020 — to F5 (222 requests), Alexeev (175), Sysoev (197), Konovalov (199) — totaling ~793 document requests revealing Lynwood's complete case theory
findings.detail: Document 103-2 (filed 09/28/2020) is Lynwood's First Request for Production. It is structured as four parallel RFPs covering: (1) F5's due diligence failures in the $670M acquisition, (2) NGINX code authorship/ownership disputes, (3) concealed pre-2012 commercialization efforts hidden from Rambler, (4) the Russian Criminal Investigation (Case No. 11901450149005396), (5) Rambler/Sberbank IP claims, (6) evidence destruction by defendants, (7) server locations and development infrastructure. The merger involved F5, Nginx Inc (BVI), Neva Merger Sub Limited, and Fortis Advisors LLC.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Paul Goldstein co-counsel - copyright ownership theory bears his academic fingerprint
findings.detail: Paul Goldstein (Stanford Law School, CA SBN 79613, paulgold@stanford.edu) is listed as co-counsel for F5, NGINX Inc (BVI), and NGINX Software Inc. Goldstein is one of the foremost U.S. copyright scholars. His involvement is reflected in several sophisticated copyright arguments: (1) The Jacobsen v. Kamind Assocs citation (535 F.3d 1373, Fed. Cir. 2008) about open source licenses and the obligation to identify original vs contributed code - this is a foundational open source copyright case; (2) The Computer Assocs v. Altai abstraction-filtration-comparison framework (982 F.2d 693, 2d Cir. 1992) for identifying protectable elements in software; (3) The argument that Lynwood Copyrighted Works definition extends BEYOND copyright scope to include ideas not reduced to writing and other IP rights appurtenant thereto, which is a sophisticated doctrinal distinction between copyright and other IP; (4) The choice-of-law analysis in footnote 6 about whether Russian or US copyright law applies, citing Itar-Tass v. Russian Kurier on the most significant relationship test; (5) The Feist/originality framework applied to the open source context; (6) The ownership-repudiation time-bar theory under Aalmuhammed v. Lee. These arguments collectively construct a framework where open source publication effectively extinguishes or at minimum complicates any employer copyright claim.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: NGINX Plus treated as post-departure development, no concession of Rambler-era work on commercial product
findings.detail: F5's brief draws a crucial line on NGINX Plus that the 9th Circuit later found insufficient. F5's Glossary defines NGINX Plus as 'A commercial version of the NGINX software with added features for paying subscribers' and NGINX BVI as 'The company that began developing NGINX Plus in 2011 and licensed the software from 2013 to 2019.' The brief's entire framework treats all commercial NGINX activity as post-departure (post-2011). Key characterizations: (1) Lynwood definition of Copyrighted Works includes 'all NGINX Plus software modules conceived and/or developed before the end of 2011' but F5 attacks this as impermissibly vague rather than substantively addressing whether any NGINX Plus code was in fact developed at Rambler pre-departure; (2) F5 notes the complaint alleges first step in the conspiracy was registering NGINXPLUS.COM in 2010 (Compl para 34, 232) - this is actually a factual concession that NGINX Plus planning began BEFORE Sysoev left Rambler in 2011; (3) F5 notes NGINX Plus commercial rollout was 2013 (Compl para 46); (4) The brief argues NGINX BVI was formed in 2011 and began developing NGINX Plus then. The 9th Circuit later found that Lynwood had plausibly alleged that at least some NGINX Plus code was conceived or developed while the team was still at Rambler, which was sufficient to survive the MTD on the copyright claim.

findings.summary: F5 argues all fraud-based claims (Claims 1, 9, 10, 13-14, 18-24) fail Rule 9(b) heightened pleading: Lynwood fails to specify WHO stole equipment, WHAT equipment, WHERE, WHEN, and HOW evidence was destroyed; fails to identify specific misrepresentations by each defendant; fails to allege Rambler actually relied on any misrepresentation or would have behaved differently
findings.detail: Section I (Doc 88, pp.20-24) attacks the fraud-based claims under Rule 9(b). Multiple sub-arguments: (A) Claims 14 (fraud), 9 (aiding/abetting), 1 (conspiracy), 10/13 (tortious interference): Lynwood alleges in 'boilerplate fashion' that NGINX Software Inc. and NGINX BVI 'engaged in fraud by directing the theft of Rambler's equipment and destruction of evidence' (Compl. para 682). F5 says this fails to specify: what actions the entities took to direct theft, which defendant stole what equipment, where each piece was stolen from, when, and how; similarly fails to allege what actions were taken to destroy evidence, where evidence was destroyed, when, and how. Also fails to explain what F5 Networks substantially assisted or knew about, and how it substantially assisted. F5 argues the complaint also fails to allege RELIANCE -- Lynwood does not allege Rambler 'actually relied on the alleged misrepresentations' or that 'any such reliance was justifiable' or that 'Rambler would have behaved differently had the omission been disclosed.' F5 notes Rambler was a 'sophisticated technology company' that knew about NGINX's world-wide popularity and paid Sysoev bonuses for it. (B) Trademark fraud (Claims 18-23): F5 argues Lynwood fails to plead that Rambler had 'clearly established' rights in the NGINX mark that were 'known to any signatory' of the trademark applications at the time the oath was signed. (C) False advertising fraud (Claim 24): fails to identify the specific false statements, which defendant made which statement, and the time and place of the alleged false advertising.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Unjust enrichment fails - F5 paid fair market value of 670M, no quasi-contractual relationship with Rambler/Lynwood
findings.detail: F5 Section V (pp.34-35) argues unjust enrichment fails for two reasons: (A) NO VIABLE THEORY: Under California law unjust enrichment is not a standalone cause of action and can only survive as a quasi-contract claim. But there is no prior quasi-contractual relationship between Lynwood/Rambler and any F5 Entity. The lack of any prior relationship precludes the application of an unjust enrichment theory. (B) ELEMENTS NOT PLED: Lynwood fails to show (1) F5 received a benefit and (2) unjust retention at Lynwood expense. The only benefits alleged are revenues and profits related to NGINX BVI (Compl para 872), but F5 obtained those benefits by paying fair market value of 670M to acquire NGINX BVI. Citing Rheem Mfg v. United States: defendant paid the fair market value of the property at the trustee sale, tends to show that there was no unjust enrichment. Even if unjust enrichment existed, restitution would go to NGINX BVI (the seller), not Lynwood.

findings.summary: F5 MTD Doc 88: Konovalov NDA obligation would end 3 years after termination, per Lynwood own allegations
findings.detail: In Section IV.D (p.47), F5 cites Lynwood own complaint paragraph 86 noting that Konovalov NDA obligation would end three years after the termination of the employment. Since Konovalov left Rambler in 2011, his NDA expired around 2014 - five years before the F5 acquisition and six years before the lawsuit. F5 uses this to argue that no existing contract was in force during the alleged interference in 2019. Additionally, F5 notes that NGINX BVI warranted to F5 Networks that NGINX BVI owned the NGINX Software outright and that no NGINX BVI employee was breaching any duty owed to any former employer (Compl para 415) - meaning Konovalov and others represented clean hands to F5 during acquisition.

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Lanham Act Standing and Laches
findings.summary: F5 argues Lynwood lacks standing for ALL Lanham Act claims (18-25) because neither Lynwood nor Rambler used the NGINX mark in commerce; trademark rights require bona fide use, not just conception by an employee. Laches bars claims because Lynwood was aware of defendants' use since at least 2004-2015 yet waited until after $670M acquisition to sue. Prejudice shown: NGINX BVI raised $100M, F5 paid $670M ($14.5M to trade name, $509M goodwill).
findings.detail: Section II (Doc 88, pp.24-32) makes multiple Lanham Act arguments: STANDING (Section II.A): (1) Trademark infringement (Claim 25): Lynwood does not allege it owns a federal registration, owns an unregistered mark, or is a non-owner with cognizable interest. Its claim rests on alleged unregistered common law rights (Compl. para 856), but common law rights require 'bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade.' Lynwood fails to allege it or Rambler used the mark in commerce independently of Sysoev. F5 argues that even if Sysoev conceived the mark within scope of employment, 'merely inventing a mark does not confer mark ownership' (Sengoku Works v. RMC Int'l). Paradoxically, Lynwood suggests Sysoev's use inured to Rambler's benefit while also alleging such use was 'unauthorized, uncontrolled, and in contravention of Sysoev's employment obligations.' F5 says Lynwood cannot have it both ways. (2) After Sysoev left in 2011, Rambler abandoned the mark -- complaint concedes NGINX website was NOT hosted on Rambler's servers after Sysoev's departure (Compl. para 516). (3) False advertising (Claim 24): Lynwood does not allege it or Rambler lost any business due to deceptive advertising. Neither sells NGINX products, so no competitive injury. (4) Cancellation claims (Claims 18-23): Lynwood has not alleged injury from continued registration; it does not sell, market, license, or commercially exploit any product by the NGINX name. STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS (Section II.D): Registration Nos. 4,196,757 and 4,200,791 issued in 2012; No. 4,837,175 issued in 2015. Three-year limitations period for fraud-based cancellation claims expired before June 2020 filing. LACHES (Section II.E): (1) Unreasonable delay: Conduct began as early as 2004 when Sysoev released under NGINX mark; 2010 NGINXPLUS.COM registration; 2011 company formation; 2012 first trademark registration; 2013 commercial NGINX Plus launch. 'Neither Lynwood nor Rambler took any action for seven years or more, far longer than any applicable limitations period.' Lynwood was aware of defendants' mark use (Compl. paras 215, 282, 520). Lynwood had constructive notice of 2012 trademark registration (Compl. para 767). In January 2015, Lynwood entered assignment agreement with Rambler 'after Sysoev appeared in industry specific media outlets to give interviews concerning his authorship' (Compl. para 471). Thus aware by 2015 at latest but waited another 5 years. (2) Prejudice: NGINX BVI raised $100M in venture funding on NGINX Plus; F5 paid $670M with $14.5M to trade name, $509M to goodwill; NGINX market share grew from 6% to exceed Apache competitor.

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Evidence Destruction & Yam Server
findings.summary: F5 does NOT deny the Yam Server allegations or evidence destruction. Instead, F5 attacks Lynwood's failure to plead the destruction with Rule 9(b) particularity -- who destroyed evidence, where, when, how. F5 treats equipment theft and evidence destruction as mere boilerplate allegations lacking specifics, but conspicuously never offers an alternative explanation for the Yam Server or disputes that equipment was taken.
findings.detail: Doc 88 references Lynwood's allegations about equipment theft and evidence destruction in Section I.A (pp.20-22). F5's argument is purely procedural, not substantive. Lynwood alleges NGINX Software Inc. and NGINX BVI 'engaged in fraud by directing the theft of Rambler's equipment and destruction of evidence' (Compl. para 682). F5 attacks this as 'boilerplate' lacking specificity under Rule 9(b) but does not deny the underlying factual allegations. F5 demands Lynwood specify: what actions were taken to direct the theft, which defendant stole what equipment, where each piece was stolen from, when, and how; who destroyed the evidence, where, when, and how. CRITICAL OBSERVATION: This is a strategic non-denial. A motion to dismiss tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint, not the facts, so F5 is not required to deny facts here. But the absence of any affirmative counter-narrative about the Yam Server or equipment -- compared to their detailed counter-narratives about NGINX's open source release and Rambler's acquiescence -- is notable. F5 was willing to construct an affirmative factual narrative about Sysoev's authorship and Rambler's knowledge, but chose not to address the Yam Server or equipment allegations substantively.

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Employment Claims Preemption
findings.summary: F5 argues all employment-related claims (conspiracy, aiding/abetting, tortious interference, fraud, unjust enrichment) are preempted by the Copyright Act because their gravamen is unauthorized use of copyrighted software. Also argues CUTSA supersedes as independent ground. Employment duties ended in 2011-2012 so all claims are time-barred under 2-3 year California statutes of limitations.
findings.detail: Section IV (Doc 88, pp.39-50) contains three independent grounds to dismiss employment claims: (A) COPYRIGHT PREEMPTION: Copyright preemption applies where (1) the work is within copyright subject matter (17 USC 102-103) and (2) state law rights are equivalent to Copyright Act Section 106 exclusive rights (Montz v. Pilgrim Films, 649 F.3d 975 (9th Cir. 2011)). F5 argues both are met because the work is computer software and all claims seek to vindicate rights in that software. No claim has an 'extra element' transforming it beyond copyright: (1) Aiding/abetting claim (Claim 9) against F5 Networks is based on aiding former employees in selling copyrighted work -- no extra element (citing Del Madera Props. v. Rhodes & Gardner); (2) Fraud claim (Claim 14) is equivalent to copyright where predicated on defendant's knowing taking of plaintiff's alleged work, not a specific misrepresentation (citing Design Art v. Nat'l Football League Props.); (3) Conspiracy, tortious interference, and unjust enrichment claims all rely on allegedly unauthorized distribution and sale of copyrighted software (citing Wilder v. CBS Corp.; Crafty Prods. v. Michaels Cos.). (B) CUTSA SUPERSESSION: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act supersedes all 'other civil remedies based upon misappropriation of confidential and proprietary information' regardless of whether information meets the statutory definition of trade secret or is copyrightable (citing Avago Techs.; Epicor Software; Mattel v. MGA). CUTSA supersedes even where no trade secret claim is pled (citing NetApp v. Nimble Storage). The employment-related claims arise from alleged theft, disclosure, and use of 'Rambler's confidential and proprietary information (proprietary NGINX Software).' (C) F5 COULD NOT HAVE KNOWN: F5 purchased NGINX in 2019; any employment breaches occurred in 2011-2012. F5 could not have aided/abetted breaches that predated its involvement by nearly a decade. NGINX BVI warranted to F5 that it owned the software outright and no employee was breaching any duty (Compl. para 415). (D) TIME BAR: California statute of limitations for interference, breach of duty of loyalty, and aiding/abetting is 2 years; for NGINX BVI/Software Inc. claims, 2-3 years. All conduct accrued in 2011 when employees allegedly joined 'conspiracy' (Compl. paras 536-537). Even if discovered later, Rambler knew or should have known by 2015 (Compl. paras 244, 471, 541).

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Key Timeline Admissions
findings.summary: F5's MTD contains critical timeline admissions drawn from complaint allegations: Sysoev at Rambler 2000-2011 (hired as sysadmin); first NGINX code 2001; open source release 2004; NGINXPLUS.COM domain registered 2010; NGINX Software Inc. and NGINX Inc. (BVI) formed 2011; first NGINX trademark registration 2012; NGINX Plus commercial launch 2013; Lynwood-Rambler assignment January 2015; NGINX BVI raised $100M VC; F5 acquisition May 2019 for $670M ($14.5M trade name, $509M goodwill); Rambler-Lynwood assignment of rights 2015.
findings.detail: Compiling all timeline points F5 accepts or references from the complaint without dispute: PRE-DEPARTURE PERIOD: - ~2000: Sysoev hired at Rambler as systems administrator (Compl. para 11) - 2001: Sysoev wrote first line of NGINX code (Compl. para 11) - Sysoev's job titles always involved 'programming' and 'system administration' (Compl. para 508) - Sysoev was 'tasked with developing software to address technical issues experienced by Rambler at the time' (Compl. para 98) - Employment agreement stated '[a]s part of the Employee's performance of his official duties, he may be entrusted with the Business Entity's administration or his or her authorized person to create works that are objects of copyright, such as computer programs and databases' (Compl. para 113) - 2004: Sysoev published NGINX as open source with BSD-style license, inserting copyright notice in his own name without mentioning Rambler (Compl. paras 21, 305) - Post-2004: Rambler gave Sysoev salary increases and bonuses (Compl. paras 21, 191) - 2007+: worldwide developers editing and improving NGINX open source code (Compl. paras 164, 171) - 2010: NGINX already had 6% global market share (Compl. para 173); NGINXPLUS.COM domain registered (Compl. paras 34, 232) DEPARTURE AND COMMERCIAL ERA: - 2011: Sysoev left Rambler (Compl. paras 280-81); NGINX Software Inc. and NGINX Inc. (BVI) formed (Compl. paras 273, 313-14, 337-38); former employees began shopping software in Silicon Valley (Compl. paras 35, 44, 238) - August 28, 2012: First NGINX trademark registration issued (Compl. para 767) - 2012: Sysoev appeared in media interviews about NGINX authorship (RJN Ex. B) - 2013: NGINX Plus commercial product launched; became 'primary driver of revenue for NGINX BVI' through 2019 (Compl. para 47) - January 2015: Rambler assigned rights to Lynwood 'after Sysoev appeared in industry specific media outlets to give interviews concerning his authorship' (Compl. para 471); Lynwood identifies itself as 'holding company' in Limassol, Cyprus (Compl. para 470) - 2015: Registration No. 4,837,175 issued (Compl. para 796) - NGINX BVI raised $100M in venture funding (Compl. para 47) - Konovalov's NDA obligation would end three years after termination (Compl. para 86) - May 2019: F5 Networks acquired NGINX companies for $670M; allocated $14.5M to trade name, $509M to goodwill (Compl. paras 55, 404-05). NGINX BVI warranted to F5 that it owned software outright and no employee was breaching any duty owed to former employer (Compl. para 415). - 2019: Rambler/Lynwood allegedly learned of 'scheme' via whistleblower (Compl. para 455)

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Open Source vs NGINX Plus Distinction
findings.summary: F5's MTD draws a critical but potentially self-defeating distinction between open source NGINX and proprietary NGINX Plus. Glossary defines NGINX Plus as 'a commercial version of the NGINX software with added features for paying subscribers' developed from 2011 by NGINX BVI. But Lynwood's copyright claim covers BOTH, and F5 never argues NGINX Plus was developed entirely independently of any Rambler-era code.
findings.detail: F5's own glossary (Doc 88, p.15) makes key definitional distinctions: NGINX = 'Web server software that Sysoev began developing in 2001 and publicly released under an open source license in 2004'; NGINX Plus = 'A commercial version of the NGINX software with added features for paying subscribers'; NGINX BVI = 'The company that began developing NGINX Plus in 2011 and licensed the software from 2013 to 2019.' F5's copyright arguments focus on the open source NGINX code -- arguing it entered the public domain via BSD license and community contributions make ownership implausible. But Lynwood's Copyrighted Works definition ALSO covers 'all NGINX Plus software modules conceived and/or developed before the end of 2011' and all derivative works. F5 never specifically argues that NGINX Plus contains no code from the Rambler era. The only argument about NGINX Plus specificity is that Lynwood's definition is too broad because it covers 'any or all post-2011 versions, releases, improvements and/or derivations' including NGINX Plus, NGINX Amplify, NGINX Controller, and NGINX Unit. This is a gap in F5's argument: if some NGINX Plus code originated during the Rambler employment period (2001-2011), the open-source-defeat-ownership argument would not apply to that proprietary code. The complaint alleges NGINX Plus modules were 'conceived and/or developed before the end of 2011' -- i.e., during Rambler employment. F5 does not rebut this.

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - F5 Acquisition Due Diligence
findings.summary: F5's MTD reveals key facts about the 2019 acquisition: NGINX BVI warranted to F5 that it owned NGINX software outright and that no NGINX BVI employee was breaching any duty owed to a former employer. F5 argues it had no actual knowledge of any employment breaches. Lynwood's allegations of F5's knowledge are characterized as mere boilerplate ('known or should have known').
findings.detail: Section IV.C.2-3 (Doc 88, pp.44-46) reveals important facts about the F5 acquisition and its due diligence: (1) NGINX BVI represented to F5 Networks that 'NGINX BVI owned the NGINX Software outright and that no NGINX BVI employee was breaching any duty owed to any former employer' (Compl. para 415). This is a significant factual admission -- it means either NGINX BVI knowingly made a false warranty, or genuinely believed it owned the software. (2) F5 argues it could not have known about or assisted breaches that occurred in 2011-2012, nearly a decade before its involvement. (3) F5 characterizes Lynwood's allegations of F5's knowledge as vague boilerplate: 'As a result of the due diligence, F5 knew about the Disloyal Employees' obligations to Rambler and the Team's fraudulent conduct against Rambler' (Compl. para 618); 'As a sophisticated entity with international offices, F5 also knew that the Disloyal Employees' obligations were ongoing and postdated their respective separations from Rambler' (Compl. para 619); 'F5 knew that the Disloyal Employees would be violating those obligations to Rambler' (Compl. para 620). F5 argues these are conclusory and insufficient -- 'Nowhere does Lynwood allege that F5 Networks actually knew of the former employee's alleged misrepresentations or that NGINX BVI's sale to F5 Networks would breach the NDA, work-for-hire, and disclosure obligations the former employees supposedly still owed Rambler over seven years after their employment had ended.' KEY QUESTION: What did F5's due diligence actually uncover about the Rambler-era development? The warranty language suggests F5 asked about prior employer claims and was told there were none.

findings.target_name: F5 Networks MTD - Fraudulent Concealment Defense
findings.summary: F5 argues NGINX BVI and NGINX Software Inc. owed no duty to disclose anything to Rambler because they had no fiduciary or transactional relationship with Rambler. They were separate competitor entities. Lynwood itself acknowledges the alleged facts were not concealed but 'rather known and accessible to persons including Rambler' and known by third-party whistleblowers.
findings.detail: Section IV.F (Doc 88, pp.48-49) addresses the fraudulent concealment claim (Claim 14). F5's argument: (1) A duty to disclose arises only from (a) a fiduciary relationship or (b) a transactional relationship where facts were actively concealed or misrepresented by omission (citing Hoffman, 228 Cal. App. 4th at 1187). (2) NGINX BVI and NGINX Software Inc. 'were, as Lynwood admits, competitors with no fiduciary or confidential ties to it or Rambler and thus owed them no duty to disclose' (Compl. paras 536-54). (3) Lynwood does not allege NGINX BVI and NGINX Software Inc. 'transacted at all with Rambler or Lynwood.' (4) Crucially, 'as Lynwood acknowledges, the alleged facts were not concealed, but rather known and accessible to persons -- including Rambler -- other than NGINX BVI and NGINX Software, Inc.' (Compl. para 224, stating the Team knew the alleged facts; Compl. paras 455-67, stating facts were known by third-party whistleblower). This is a significant factual point: F5 is arguing that Rambler knew what was happening all along, and the concealment claim is contradicted by Lynwood's own allegations. NOTE: The mention of the footnote 9 concession on 'misrepresenting their true intentions to commercialize products' (Compl. para 683) applying only to former employees, not F5 entities, is also important -- F5 separates itself from the individual defendants' alleged concealment.

findings.target_name: NGINX Inc / Igor Sysoev / Maxim Konovalov
findings.summary: 2011 pre-departure commercialization cluster: company formation, VC term sheet, and Sysoev coding withdrawal all within 7 months
findings.detail: The entire pre-departure commercialization effort completed in 7 months while founders remained Rambler employees: (1) April 2011: Series A term sheet with Runa Capital and BV Capital finalized; pitch deck names F5 as exit target. (2) May 4, 2011: NGINX Software Inc (Delaware) incorporated. (3) July 6, 2011: Nginx, Inc. (BVI) -- actual parent entity -- incorporated. (4) August 2011: Runa Capital leads M Series A. (5) Late 2011: Sysoev and Konovalov depart Rambler. (6) December 2011: Sysoev drops from 281 commits/year to 8 in 2012 -- coding ends as management begins. The BVI incorporation (July 6) occurred 3 months before reported departure.

findings.summary: Sysoev silence period 2012-2017: 11 commits over 5 years vs 281 in 2011 alone -- transition from developer to figurehead at corporate formation
findings.detail: Igor Sysoev's commit history shows a dramatic and permanent discontinuity in 2011-2012 coinciding exactly with NGINX Inc formation: 281 commits in 2011 (pre-departure) -> 8 commits in 2012 -> 0 in 2013 -> 0 in 2014 -> 1 in 2015 -> 2 in 2016 -> 0 in 2017. Total 5-year output: 11 commits. He remained CTO of NGINX Inc and later F5 until 2022 but contributed no meaningful code. This is the pattern of a founder who became an executive/figurehead post-commercialization -- or who was prohibited from or uninterested in contributing once the financial structure was in place. Sysoev's BVI company (Hogwarts United S.A., Pandora Papers) and his departure from coding parallel the company formation timeline.

findings.summary: NGINX Software, Inc. (Delaware) is the highest-centrality zero-finding node in the nginx graph: betweenness rank 5 of 29 (0.373), degree=2, 0 findings. It bridges the Runa Capital investment cluster to the Nginx Inc BVI corporate chain, making it structurally critical but entirely uninvestigated. This is the primary corporate coverage gap.
findings.detail: NGINX Software, Inc. is the Delaware operating entity that received the Runa Capital Series A investment (Aug 2011). It is also linked to Nginx Inc (BVI) which is the parent of BV NGINX LLC, NGINX International Ltd, and Nginx Asia Pacific Pte Ltd. findings.detail: Triadic closure analysis identifies the Chikhachev-Beloussov triad via Runa Capital as the most likely undocumented direct relationship (score=0.75 out of 1.0). The absence of a documented direct link may reflect: (1) research gap (they obviously know each other as co-founders — the connection exists, we haven't documented it); (2) a deliberate arm's-length arrangement if their roles are compartmentalized. Action needed: document the Chikhachev-Beloussov direct relationship and check for any separate vehicles or structures they operate together outside Runa Capital.
